reading.body:
AI adoption in US churches is not tracked by any official census; it is measured by a patchwork of research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes.

The pattern is measurement by survey and platform rather than by census. Barna Group runs the closest thing to sector-wide survey data, Gloo reports deployment across thousands of US churches, and Hartford and Pew add congregational and public attitude data. Census BTOS includes religious and civic organisations in its service-sector series, but no better official measure exists yet.

This matters for AI because adoption in churches is real but diffuse, and every tradition is writing its own guidance. The data does not say how many congregations actually use AI, how much compute that use requires, or what it means for power demand. It also does not give a single adoption rate, because none exists.

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The official measure for this sector comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which covers religious organizations inside its other services grouping under NAICS 81. The most recent figure is 15.0%, up from 13.7% in the prior period, and the survey question asks whether the business used AI in the last two weeks. The Census Bureau first asked this question in September 2023. That is the only quantified adoption number in the material, and it covers a broad service-sector category rather than congregations alone.

On what AI is actually used for, the harvested pages are thinner than the adoption figure. Barna Group, described as a Christian research organization tracking trends in faith, culture and ministry, reports that nearly all pastors say a church should have guidelines for responsible AI use, while far fewer say their own church does. That gap between stated principle and written policy is the clearest finding in the source material about practice. Gloo, which the curated points describe as used by thousands of US churches, presents its AI offering as values-aligned models, developer tools and benchmarks for faith-based organizations, with API-first support for inference, retrieval-augmented generation and assistant workflows, and dynamic selection of the appropriate model for each request. The curated points frame the sector's use cases as sermon prep, administration and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations.

Where vendors and money concentrate is only partly visible here. Gloo is the named platform, and its page describes AI as a foundational capability across its platform to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry and create practical value across the faith and flourishing ecosystem. AI and Faith appears as a nonprofit network rather than a vendor, convening faith leaders, scholars, technologists, ethicists and educators, and it notes that 85 percent of the world's population claims a religious affiliation, which it uses to argue that the world's religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide AI development. It solicits tax-deductible donations. No dollar figures, funding totals or market sizes appear in the material.

The sources report no ROI evidence for this sector. Nothing in the excerpts quantifies cost savings, time saved or revenue effects from AI in churches. The closest material is qualitative and comes from the University of Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, whose director is Meghan Sullivan. A white paper from All Tech is Human and the Notre Dame-IBM Technology Ethics lab, titled Two Views of the Same Transformation, found that mid-level professionals described checking AI output as a growing, unrecognized share of their work, with some calling it babysitting AI slop, that this glue work of a rollout is missing from performance reviews, and that women reported carrying more of it. Executives in the same study described middle management as a layer to cut, then worried about distributed deskilling. Sullivan, a Catholic philosopher, said many workers in the industry talk very flippantly about job displacement and AI doing work faster and cheaper.

The regulatory posture in this material is ethical and voluntary rather than legal. AI and Faith frames the issues as deeply moral and, for religiously affiliated populations, deeply spiritual, and seeks to inject humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected them both. Notre Dame's institute promotes interdisciplinary research and policy leadership in AI and other technology ethics, engaging stakeholders to provide practical models and applied solutions for ethical technology design, development and deployment. Barna's finding that pastors overwhelmingly want guidelines but few churches have them points the same direction, toward self-governance rather than external rules. Pew Research Center's religion work appears in the material mainly on religious hostilities and demographics, including that 55 countries had high or very high levels of social hostilities involving religion in 2023, up from 45 the previous year, and that converts make up 8% of U.S. Catholics, with no AI-specific finding on its page.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few modest conclusions. Adoption in the Census Bureau's broader services category sits at 15.0%, so this is not a sector where AI use is universal or assumed. The named infrastructure exists, chiefly Gloo, and the ethics conversation is organized, chiefly through AI and Faith and Notre Dame. The most actionable finding is Barna's: the demand for responsible-use guidelines is near universal among pastors while actual guidelines are not, which suggests policy work is the unmet step. Hartford Institute for Religion Research is described as having a 45 year history of accurate research on churches and congregational life and as regularly surveying congregational trends and digital adoption, but its page as harvested contains no figures, so nothing further can be said from it.

https://ethics.nd.edu/.brief: The Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, brings together a multidisciplinary community to advance moral understanding and respond to pressing ethical issues, including work on artificial intelligence and technology ethics that engages stakeholders to develop practical models for ethical design and deployment. A white paper from All Tech is Human and the Notre Dame-IBM Technology Ethics lab, titled Two Views of the Same Transformation, reported that mid-level professionals described checking AI output as a growing and unrecognised part of their jobs, with some calling it "babysitting AI slop." That paper also found the glue work of a rollout is absent from performance reviews and that women reported carrying more of it, while executives described middle management as a layer to cut and then worried about distributed deskilling. Sullivan, a Catholic philosopher at the University of Notre Dame who often meets AI leaders and developers, said many workers in the industry talk very flippantly about job displacement and about AI doing work faster and cheaper, and that some are trying to transcend work to spend their time on family and hobbies such as gardening and crafts.

https://www.barna.com/.brief: Barna Group describes itself as a Christian research organisation producing data and insights on trends affecting faith, culture and ministry, alongside articles, reports, podcasts, courses and services. New Barna research examined how pastors use AI and where guidelines might apply. According to that research, nearly all pastors believe a church should have guidelines for responsible AI use, while far fewer report that their own church has them.

https://www.gloo.us/ai.brief: According to Gloo, its AI offering provides models, developer tools, and benchmarks that are aligned with the values of faith-based organizations. The company describes AI as a foundational capability across its platform, intended to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry, and create practical value. Developers using Gloo AI Studio can access connected infrastructure including production environment tools, trusted content, and values-aligned models. The platform also offers API-first support for inference, RAG, and assistant workflows, with dynamic selection of the appropriate model for each request.

https://aiandfaith.org/.brief: AI and Faith describes itself as a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators and partner organisations working toward a future in which AI serves humankind under five strategic pillars. The organisation argues that these issues are deeply moral at root, and ,  for the 85 percent of the world's population it says claims a religious affiliation ,  deeply spiritual too, with the world's religions offering ancient wisdom to guide AI's development and use. It says it encourages, connects and equips tech creators, academic researchers, ethicists and theologians to engage with the moral and ethical questions around AI and related technologies, aiming to shape the discussion in thoughtful, life-affirming ways. A statement quoted on the page frames the goal as injecting "humility and historicity" into an industry that has often rejected both, and as a humanistic effort to bring faith-based, literary, classical and oral traditions to bear on what it calls possibly the most important technological transformation of our time.
